questions.lead_in: Based on the Gram stain, what is the most appropriate stain to perform?
questions.explanation: Modified acid-fast The Gram stain shows filamentous beaded gram-positive rods, indicative of an aerobic actinomycete, most closely resembling Nocardia. A modified acid-fast stain would be positive for Nocardia. A positive modified acid-fast stain result would not provide a definitive diagnosis since other aerobic actinomycetes can be modified acid-fast positive. However, based on the other factors, it supports the diagnosis of nocardiosis while waiting for the organism to grow in culture. The acid-fast stain is for Mycobacterium spp. Nocardia will stain negative with the acid-fast stain, as it uses a stronger decolorizing agent. Giemsa, periodic acid–Schiff, and Warthin–Starry are histopathology stains that are unrelated to the diagnosis of aerobic actinomycetes.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q1

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman was admitted with pneumonia following influenza A infection. IV ceftriaxone was started empirically. Investigations: Sputum culture: Staphylococcus aureus isolated; resistant to clindamycin, sensitive to oxacillin, trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX), and vancomycin
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate method for ceftriaxone susceptibility testing?
questions.explanation: Susceptibility can be inferred Oxacillin is an indicator drug for determining MSSA vs. MRSA. Breakpoints do not exist for other beta-lactam drugs for staphylococci, and testing other beta-lactams can lead to inaccurate results. Oxacillin-susceptible staphylococci are susceptible to nafcillin, cephalosporins, beta-lactam/ beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, and carbapenems. Because the isolate is susceptible to oxacillin, it can be inferred that it is also susceptible to ceftriaxone.

questions.question: The Gram stain.
questions.question_raw: Gram stains.

parts.text: Describe the method.
Four organisms that do not stain well.
Two organisms that tend to overdecolourize.
What are two tests that can be done to differentiate a gram-positive from a gram-negative organism if the stain is equivocal?

parts_raw.text: Describe the method.
4 organisms that don't stain well.
2 organisms that tend to overdecolourize
What are 2 tests that can be done to differentiate a gram positive from a gram negative organism (if the stain is equivocal)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Prepare a thin smear, air dry, fix (heat or methanol; methanol preserves morphology and is preferred). Flood with crystal violet 1 min, rinse. Apply Gram iodine mordant 1 min, rinse - forms crystal violet-iodine complex in the cell. Decolourize with acetone-alcohol 1-5 s until runoff is clear, rinse immediately. Counterstain with safranin (or basic fuchsin, better for pale gram-negatives) 30-60 s, rinse, blot dry, read under oil at 1000x. Gram-positives have thick cross-linked peptidoglycan that traps the complex (purple); gram-negatives have thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane dissolved by the decolourizer, so they take up counterstain (pink). Include a QC control smear (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus/Escherichia coli) with each stain batch.
b) (1) Mycobacterium species - waxy mycolic acid cell wall (appear as unstained "ghosts"). (2) Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma - no cell wall. (3) Legionella species - poorly staining gram-negative; needs prolonged basic fuchsin counterstain. (4) Spirochetes (Treponema, Leptospira, Borrelia) - too thin to resolve by light microscopy. Also acceptable: Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Coxiella, Bartonella, Ehrlichia/Anaplasma (obligate intracellular), Tropheryma whipplei.
c) (1) Clostridium species (notably C. tertium, C. ramosum, C. clostridioforme) - stain gram-variable or frankly gram-negative, especially in older cultures. (2) Bacillus species in older/sporulating cultures. Also acceptable: Peptostreptococcus, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mobiluncus, Listeria in aged cultures.
d) (1) 3% KOH string test - gram-negatives lyse and the suspension becomes viscous/strings on lifting the loop; gram-positives do not. (2) Antibiotic disc test on a lawn of the isolate: vancomycin 5 microgram (any zone = gram-positive) with colistin/polymyxin B 10 microgram (zone = gram-negative). Also acceptable: L-alanine aminopeptidase (LAP) test - positive in gram-negatives; aminopeptidase or MALDI-TOF identification.

questions.question: A lung biopsy is sent from a patient who is immunocompromised. They are concerned about a fungal infection and have sent for fungal culture.
questions.question_raw: A lung biopsy is sent from a patient who is immunocompromised. They are concerned about a fungal infection and have sent for fungal culture.

parts.text: How would you process the specimen in the lab?
What are three media you would use, and provide a rationale for each?
What are two media you could use to enhance sporulation?

parts_raw.text: How would you process the specimen in the lab?
What are 3 media you would use and provide a rationale for each?
What are 2 media you could use to enhance sporulation?

questions.model_answer:
a) Handle all manipulation in a class II biological safety cabinet (BSL-2; BSL-3 practices once a dimorphic mould is suspected). Keep the tissue moist with sterile saline; do not let it dry. Mince/tease the tissue finely with a sterile scalpel or tissue grinder - do NOT homogenize or grind when a Mucorales is possible, since grinding destroys the fragile aseptate hyphae and gives a false-negative culture. Divide the specimen: (i) direct microscopy - calcofluor white/KOH, Gram stain, and histopathology with GMS and PAS on the paraffin block; (ii) culture - inoculate the minced tissue onto the surface of solid media (do not embed), plus a broth if desired; (iii) hold tissue/reserve for bacterial, mycobacterial and molecular testing (panfungal PCR, Aspergillus and Mucorales PCR). Incubate at 30 C (and a duplicate set at 35-37 C for dimorphic and thermophilic species such as Aspergillus fumigatus and Mucorales), in air, in vented screw-cap tubes or taped plates, for up to 4 weeks, examined at least 3 times weekly. Report preliminary microscopy urgently to the clinician.
b) (1) Sabouraud dextrose agar with chloramphenicol and gentamicin - general-purpose isolation medium; low pH and antibacterials suppress bacterial overgrowth from a non-sterile-adjacent site. (2) Brain-heart infusion agar with 5-10% sheep blood and antibacterials, incubated at 35-37 C - enriched medium needed to recover the fastidious thermally dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Talaromyces) and to convert them to the yeast phase. (3) A cycloheximide-FREE medium such as inhibitory mould agar or SDA without cycloheximide - essential in the immunocompromised because cycloheximide inhibits the very opportunists expected here (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Mucorales, Scedosporium, Candida). A cycloheximide-containing plate may be run in parallel to suppress rapidly growing saprophytic contaminants when a dimorphic fungus is suspected.
c) (1) Potato dextrose (or potato flake) agar. (2) Cornmeal agar with Tween 80. Both are nutritionally poor relative to routine media, which stresses the mould and stimulates conidiation and pigment production; other acceptable answers are water agar, malt extract agar and Czapek-Dox agar.

questions.model_answer:
a) R - over 90% of isolates produce a plasmid-mediated penicillinase (blaZ); confirm apparent susceptibility with a nitrocefin/induced beta-lactamase test or zone-edge test.
b) R - Morganella morganii (like Proteus and Providencia) has intrinsically elevated imipenem MICs; meropenem or ertapenem is preferred.
c) S - trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the agent of choice for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.
d) R - Burkholderia cepacia complex (and B. pseudomallei) are intrinsically resistant to polymyxins/colistin.
e) R - Klebsiella pneumoniae carries a chromosomal SHV-1 (K. oxytoca, OXY/K1) beta-lactamase, so it is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin and amoxicillin.

questions.question: Antiviral susceptibility testing.
questions.question_raw: Antiviral susceptibility testing.

parts.text: What is the main difference between phenotypic and genotypic testing?
What are two chronic viral infections that can only be tested by genotype?
What are two chronic viral infections that can be tested both genotypically and phenotypically?
Viral cytopathic effect detection: what are three methods to detect viral growth if there is no cytopathic effect pattern?

parts_raw.text: What is the main difference between phenotypic and genotypic testing?
What are 2 chronic viral infections that can only be done by genotype?
What are 2 chronic viral infections that can be tested genotypically and phenotypically?
Viral CPE detection. What are 3 methods to detect viral growth if there is no CPE pattern?

questions.model_answer:
a) Phenotypic testing measures the functional drug concentration that inhibits viral replication (IC50/EC50) in cell culture or in a recombinant/reporter virus assay - it detects resistance from any mechanism, including novel ones, but requires a viable isolate or amplifiable gene construct, is slow (weeks), labour-intensive and available only in reference labs. Genotypic testing sequences the drug-target gene from the clinical specimen and infers resistance from known mutations - fast, cheap and done directly on plasma/blood, but only detects previously characterized mutations, requires an interpretation database, and misses minority variants below the assay's detection threshold.
b) (1) Hepatitis C virus. (2) Hepatitis B virus. Neither can be propagated in routine cell culture, so resistance testing (HCV NS3/NS5A/NS5B; HBV polymerase rtM204V/I etc.) is sequence-based only.
c) (1) HIV - genotype (reverse transcriptase, protease, integrase, gp41/gp120) and recombinant-virus phenotype (e.g. PhenoSense, Antivirogram), including phenotype-genotype virtual phenotypes and tropism assays. (2) Cytomegalovirus - UL97/UL54 (and UL56 for letermovir) sequencing plus plaque-reduction or DNA-hybridization phenotypic assay on a culture isolate. Herpes simplex virus (UL23/UL30 genotype and plaque-reduction phenotype) is an acceptable alternative.
d) (1) Haemadsorption/haemagglutination with guinea pig erythrocytes - detects influenza, parainfluenza and mumps, which express haemagglutinin before CPE appears. (2) Immunostaining of the monolayer with fluorescein- or peroxidase-labelled monoclonal antibodies (shell-vial centrifugation culture read at 16-48 h). (3) Nucleic acid detection (PCR) on the culture supernatant or cell scrapings. Other acceptable answers: interference (unmasking a non-cytopathic agent such as rubella by challenge with echovirus 11), electron microscopy of the supernatant, and blind passage onto a second cell line.

questions.question: You have been advised that the manufacturer of your blood culture bottles has had issues with false negatives from lots of blood culture bottles between January and August of 2012.
questions.question_raw: You have been advised that the manufacturer of your blood culture bottles has had issues with "false-negatives" from lots of blood culture bottles between January – August of 2012.

parts.text: What are five things you need to do?

parts_raw.text: What are 5 things you need to do?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Quarantine and stop use: identify the affected lot numbers, pull all remaining bottles of those lots from the lab and from ward/clinic stock, segregate them as "do not use", and obtain replacement lots from the manufacturer or an alternate supplier so service is not interrupted. (2) Notify and document: inform the laboratory medical director and quality manager, hospital administration/risk management, infection prevention and control, and the clinical services; open a formal non-conformance/incident report under the lab's quality management system and inform the accrediting body as required. (3) Look-back on affected patients: retrieve all blood cultures processed with the implicated lots between January and August 2012, cross-reference with concurrent positive cultures from other sites, positive molecular tests, autopsy/pathology results and patients treated empirically for sepsis, and assess whether any negative result was clinically discordant and would have changed management. (4) Retest and re-verify: terminally subculture or re-incubate any retained bottles, perform in-house verification of the current and replacement lots with seeded QC organisms (including a fastidious/slow grower such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Candida and an anaerobe) at low inoculum before release, and review instrument function, temperature, agitation and detection algorithms to exclude an additional in-house cause. (5) Disclose and report externally: notify affected patients' physicians and issue amended/qualified reports where a result may be unreliable, follow the institution's error-disclosure policy, and report the device problem to the manufacturer and to the regulator (Health Canada Medical Device Problem Report; FDA MedWatch in the US), retaining samples for their investigation.

questions.question: You want to implement a second blood culture incubator.
questions.question_raw: You want to implement a 2nd blood culture incubator.

parts.text: List two issues with verifying the new instrument.

parts_raw.text: List 2 issues with verifying the new instrument.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Obtaining enough positive material for a meaningful comparison. Verification requires parallel/split testing against the existing instrument for recovery rate and time to detection, but true positives are uncommon (roughly 5-10% of sets), and clinically important fastidious or slow-growing organisms (Haemophilus, Neisseria, Streptococcus pneumoniae, anaerobes, yeast, Brucella, HACEK) are rarer still - so seeded/simulated cultures with low inocula and spiked human blood must substitute, and these do not fully reproduce patient specimens (antibiotic-containing blood, variable fill volume, delayed entry). (2) Non-interchangeability of the two systems and the operational infrastructure around them. Bottle formulations, resin/charcoal, fill volume requirements, detection algorithms and software versions may differ between instruments, so time to detection and contamination rates are not directly comparable; you must also validate LIS/middleware interfacing and result mapping, delayed-entry and off-hours loading protocols, separate QC, maintenance, alarm and temperature monitoring, staff training and competency, plus adequate space, power and back-up - and decide how the two data streams are combined for antibiogram and contamination-rate trending.

questions.question: A chart is provided about introducing a new antimicrobial susceptibility test, giving data from the gold standard and how the new test compares to the gold standard.
questions.question_raw: Chart about introducing a new antimicrobial susceptibility test. Given data from the gold standard and how the next test compares to the gold standard.

parts.text: Calculate very major, major and minor errors, and categorical agreement.
What are the accepted errors for introducing a new test (percentage of very major errors and major errors)? What is the minimum percentage categorical agreement required of the new test?

parts_raw.text: Asked to calculate very major, major and minor errors. Also categorical agreement.
What are the accepted errors for introducing a new test (% of VME, ME)? What is the minimum % categorical agreement required of the new test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Classify every isolate by the new test result versus the reference (gold standard) result:
(1) Very major error (false susceptible; the dangerous error) = reference R, new test S. VME rate = number of VMEs divided by the number of isolates RESISTANT by the reference method x 100.
(2) Major error (false resistant) = reference S, new test R. ME rate = number of MEs divided by the number of isolates SUSCEPTIBLE by the reference method x 100.
(3) Minor error = one method reports intermediate and the other reports susceptible or resistant (S vs I, or R vs I). Minor error rate = number of minor errors divided by the TOTAL number of isolates tested x 100.
(4) Categorical agreement = number of isolates given the same S/I/R category by both methods divided by the total number tested x 100. (Essential agreement, if MICs are given, = proportion of results within plus or minus one doubling dilution of the reference MIC.)
b) Very major errors 1.5% or less (calculated on resistant isolates; up to 3% is considered marginally acceptable when challenge strains are included), major errors 3% or less (calculated on susceptible isolates), and categorical agreement at least 90%. Essential agreement must also be at least 90%. The evaluation should include a resistant challenge set so that at least 20-30% of isolates are non-susceptible.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M52 (Verification of Commercial Microbial Identification and AST Systems) and the FDA antimicrobial susceptibility test system guidance are the source of the 1.5%/3%/90% thresholds.

questions.question: Antibiograms.

parts.text: List four recommendations for analyzing and preparing antibiograms as per CLSI.

parts_raw.text: List 4 recommendations for analyzing and preparing antibiograms as per CLSI?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Analyze and present the cumulative antibiogram at least annually. (2) Include only species with at least 30 isolates tested; if fewer than 30, do not report a percentage for that organism (report the numbers or aggregate over a longer period instead). (3) Include only diagnostic isolates - exclude surveillance/screening isolates (e.g. MRSA and VRE screens) - and include only final, verified results. (4) Include only the FIRST isolate of a given species per patient per analysis period, regardless of body site or susceptibility profile. Other acceptable answers: report percent susceptible only, and do not include intermediate results in that percentage; report only antimicrobials that are routinely tested and reported for that organism; use a single reliable susceptibility test method; consider separate antibiograms by unit, specimen type or inpatient/outpatient when isolate numbers permit.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M39 (Analysis and Presentation of Cumulative Antimicrobial Susceptibility Test Data).

questions.question: Susceptibility testing of cerebrospinal fluid isolates.

parts.text: What are four antibiotics that are not recommended for routine testing in cerebrospinal fluid as per CLSI?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 antibiotics that are not recommended for routine testing in CSF as per CLSI?

questions.model_answer: a) Agents that do not reliably cross the blood-brain barrier or lack CSF breakpoints should not be routinely reported on isolates from cerebrospinal fluid: (1) clindamycin; (2) macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin); (3) tetracyclines, including doxycycline and tigecycline; (4) first- and second-generation cephalosporins and the cephamycins (cefazolin, cefoxitin, cefotetan) - with the exception of parenteral cefuroxime, and also the oral cephalosporins. Other acceptable answers: aminoglycosides, daptomycin, and oral antimicrobials generally (e.g. oral beta-lactams, nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin).

questions.question: Carbapenemase detection.

parts.text: What is a method described by CLSI to confirm a Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase? What is one example of a false positive using this test?

parts_raw.text: What is a method described by CLSI to confirm a KPC? What is 1 example of a false positive using this test?

questions.model_answer: a) Method: the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) - the test isolate is emulsified in broth with a meropenem 10 microgram disc for 4 h; the disc is then placed on a lawn of a carbapenem-susceptible Escherichia coli ATCC 25922. A carbapenemase hydrolyses the meropenem in the disc, so the indicator strain grows up to the disc (zone 6-15 mm or pinpoint colonies within 16-18 mm = carbapenemase positive). A parallel EDTA-mCIM (eCIM) distinguishes a metallo-beta-lactamase from a serine carbapenemase such as KPC. The older CLSI method was the modified Hodge test (cloverleaf indentation of the indicator strain toward a carbapenem disc), now withdrawn because of poor performance. False positive: a non-carbapenemase mechanism - an ESBL (classically a CTX-M producer) or a hyperproduced AmpC combined with outer membrane porin loss (e.g. Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella pneumoniae with OmpK35/36 loss) gives a positive modified Hodge test; mucoid strains and Enterobacter species are also classic modified Hodge test false positives. Molecular confirmation (blaKPC PCR) or an immunochromatographic lateral-flow carbapenemase assay resolves the discrepancy.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100: mCIM/eCIM are the current recommended phenotypic carbapenemase tests; the modified Hodge test was removed from M100 after 2018.

questions.question: Nucleic acid amplification methods.

parts.text: Three nucleic acid amplification methods besides polymerase chain reaction.

parts_raw.text: 3 nucleic acid amplification methods besides PCR.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Transcription-mediated amplification (TMA)/nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA) - isothermal, RNA target, uses reverse transcriptase plus T7 RNA polymerase to generate RNA amplicons (Aptima assays for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HCV, HIV viral load). (2) Strand displacement amplification (SDA) - isothermal, restriction enzyme nicks a hemiphosphorothioate site and a polymerase lacking 5' exonuclease activity displaces the strand (BD ProbeTec). (3) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) - a strand-displacing Bst polymerase with 4-6 primers producing concatemeric product at a single temperature, read by turbidity or fluorescence (Alethia/Illumigene assays for Clostridioides difficile, group B Streptococcus). Other acceptable answers: ligase chain reaction, helicase-dependent amplification, rolling-circle/whole-genome amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification. (Branched DNA and hybrid capture are signal, not target, amplification methods.)

questions.question: Your lab is using African green monkey cells for viral culture. There is a request for enterovirus culture. The tube inoculated with the patient's sample is already showing cytopathic effect after one day. On examination of other un-inoculated cells, there is already cytopathic effect. On electron microscopy, it looks like a herpesviridae.
questions.question_raw: Your lab is using African green monkey cells for viral culture. There is a request for enterovirus culture. The sample inoculated with the patient's sample is already showing CPE after 1 day. On examination of other un-inoculated cells, there is already CPE. On EM, it looks like a herpesviridae.

parts.text: What virus is causing the cytopathic effect?
What are the implications for the patient sample inoculated in the contaminated bottle?

parts_raw.text: What virus is causing the CPE?
What are the implications for the patient sample inoculated in the contaminated bottle?

questions.model_answer:
a) An adventitious (endogenous) simian herpesvirus contaminating the primary African green monkey kidney cells - simian cytomegalovirus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 5) is the classic culprit, with simian agent 8 (SA8, Cercopithecine herpesvirus 2) the alternative. It is not the patient's enterovirus: cytopathic effect in the un-inoculated control cells proves the cell line itself is contaminated, and the herpesvirus morphology on electron microscopy excludes an enterovirus (small, non-enveloped picornavirus). The other well-known contaminants of primary monkey kidney cells - simian foamy virus and SV40 - are excluded by morphology. Note the biosafety point: if the cells were macaque rather than African green monkey, B virus (Macacine herpesvirus 1) would be the concern and is a lethal occupational hazard.
b) The culture is invalid and uninterpretable - cytopathic effect in that tube cannot be attributed to the patient's specimen, so it can be read as neither a positive (false-positive enterovirus report) nor a reliable negative (the contaminant destroys the monolayer within a day and masks true growth, a false negative). Do not report a result; issue a "specimen unsuitable/culture invalid" comment, notify the clinician, and request or repeat testing. Repeat the culture on a fresh, quality-controlled lot of cells - preferably a different line suited to enterovirus (RD, A549, human fibroblast, LLC-MK2) - or, better, replace culture with an enterovirus RT-PCR, which is faster and unaffected. As a lab issue: quarantine and discard the contaminated cell lot, check whether other cultures from the same lot were affected and review/recall those reports, notify the cell-culture supplier, document as a non-conformance, and reinforce cell-line QC (uninoculated control tubes with every run, mycoplasma and adventitious-agent screening) and biosafety practice for staff exposed to a simian herpesvirus.
questions.beyond_mandell: Species-level attribution rests on the known adventitious agents of primary African green monkey kidney cell cultures; simian CMV versus SA8 cannot be separated on electron microscopy alone and requires PCR or antigen typing.

questions.question: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for organism identification.
questions.question_raw: MALDI-TOF.

parts.text: Give three bacteria or bacterial groups that MALDI-TOF has difficulty identifying.
Give one way in which these limitations can be improved.

parts_raw.text: 3 bacteria or bacterial groups that the MALDI has trouble identifying.
1 way in which these limitations can be improved.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Streptococcus pneumoniae versus the viridans/mitis group streptococci (near-identical spectra). (2) Escherichia coli versus Shigella species (and Shigella species from one another). (3) Closely related non-fermenters/other complexes — e.g. the Burkholderia cepacia complex, Acinetobacter baumannii–calcoaceticus complex, and coagulase-negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus capitis vs hominis; mycobacteria and moulds also perform poorly without extended extraction.
b) Supplement/expand the reference spectral database with well-curated, locally validated spectra and use improved extraction methods (formic acid/ethanol tube extraction, bead beating for mycobacteria and moulds), plus confirmatory phenotypic or molecular testing (optochin/bile solubility for S. pneumoniae, biochemical or 16S/targeted PCR for E. coli vs Shigella) for the known problem groups.

questions.question: Laboratory differentiation of Staphylococcus from Micrococcus.

parts.text: Give four ways to differentiate Staphylococcus from Micrococcus in the laboratory.

parts_raw.text: 4 ways to differentiate Staphylococcus and Micrococcus in the lab.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Modified oxidase (microdase): Micrococcus positive, Staphylococcus negative. (2) Bacitracin 0.04 U disk: Micrococcus susceptible, Staphylococcus resistant. (3) Furazolidone 100 µg disk: Staphylococcus susceptible, Micrococcus resistant. (4) Anaerobic/oxidative-fermentative glucose utilization: Staphylococcus ferments glucose anaerobically (acid in OF tube, growth in thioglycollate), Micrococcus is strictly oxidative. (Also: lysostaphin susceptibility — Staphylococcus lysed, Micrococcus not; colonial morphology — Micrococcus often yellow/pigmented, larger tetrads on Gram stain; MALDI-TOF readily separates the genera.)

parts.text: Gram-negative bacillus, oxidase negative, non-swarming, beta-hemolytic
Gram-negative bacillus, oxidase negative, swarming, indole positive
Gram-positive coccus, catalase negative, PYR positive

parts_raw.text: GNB, ox negative, non-swarming, beta-hemolytic
GNB, ox negative, swarming, indole positive
GPC, cat negative, PYR positive

questions.model_answer:
a) Treat as Escherichia coli: a lactose-fermenting/beta-hemolytic, oxidase-negative, non-swarming GNB on chromogenic or MacConkey medium can be identified as E. coli by spot indole (or chromogenic agar colour) alone — no further biochemical panel or MALDI needed; report with a standard urinary susceptibility panel.
b) Treat as Proteus mirabilis versus Proteus vulgaris — swarming, oxidase-negative GNB with indole positive indicates P. vulgaris (P. mirabilis is indole negative); this one warrants full identification and susceptibility testing since P. vulgaris is ampicillin/cephalosporin resistant (inducible), whereas indole-negative swarmers can be reported as P. mirabilis on spot indole alone.
c) Treat as Enterococcus species: catalase-negative, PYR-positive GPC in urine can be reported as "Enterococcus species" from PYR plus colony/Gram morphology (bile-esculin/growth in 6.5% NaCl confirm) without speciation; add ampicillin, nitrofurantoin and vancomycin susceptibilities, and reserve species-level identification/MALDI for sterile-site or vancomycin-resistant isolates. (Note: rule out Streptococcus pyogenes, also PYR positive, by beta-hemolysis and bacitracin/group A antigen.)

questions.question: Beta-lactamase testing in Staphylococcus aureus.

parts.text: For Staphylococcus aureus, what are two different methods to test for beta-lactamase production?

parts_raw.text: For Staphylococcus aureus, what are 2 different methods to test for beta-lactamase production?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Nitrocefin (chromogenic cephalosporin) disk/test on growth taken from the zone margin of a cefoxitin or penicillin disk induction — colour change from yellow to red indicates beta-lactamase. (2) Penicillin disk zone-edge test: a penicillin-susceptible MIC/zone with a sharp "cliff-edge" zone margin indicates beta-lactamase production (a fuzzy/"beach" edge is negative); alternatively detect blaZ by PCR.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 recommends induced nitrocefin plus the penicillin disk zone-edge test before reporting S. aureus as penicillin susceptible.

questions.question: MALDI-TOF is a revolutionary method for bacterial identification.
questions.question_raw: 26. MALDI-TOF is a revolutionary methods for bacterial identification

parts.text: List four characteristics of this test.
How does it work?

parts_raw.text: List 4 characteristics of this test.
b) HOW DOES IT WORK?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Rapid — identification in minutes from an isolated colony, hours to days faster than conventional biochemical panels. (2) Accurate to genus and usually species level across a very broad range of bacteria, yeasts, mycobacteria and moulds, using a large reference spectral database. (3) Inexpensive per test with low consumable cost (a target plate, matrix and formic acid) after a high capital outlay, so it is most cost-effective in high-volume laboratories. (4) Can be applied to more than isolated colonies — directly to positive blood culture broths and to urine — but it has limited ability to separate very closely related organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae vs mitis group, Escherichia coli vs Shigella) and does not provide susceptibility results.
b) Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry: a colony is spotted onto a metal target and overlaid with an organic matrix (e.g. alpha-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid), with or without formic acid/ethanol extraction. The dried co-crystal is struck by a pulsed nitrogen laser; the matrix absorbs the energy, desorbing and ionizing mainly abundant bacterial ribosomal proteins. The charged proteins are accelerated through an electric field down a vacuum flight tube, and the time of flight to the detector varies with mass-to-charge ratio (smaller ions arrive first). The resulting mass spectrum — a species-characteristic protein fingerprint — is compared with a reference database and reported with a confidence/log score.

cohort_answer.text: Large database of organisms that can be identified; Rapid; Can be used on direct patient specimens; Cost effective for bigger labs with large volume of specimens; Accurate. Disadvantage: MALDI cannot differentiate Shigella flexnerii & E coli, Strep mitis & pneumoniae.

Besides organism-related issues, name three general advantages and three general disadvantages of using MALDI-TOF in a microbiology laboratory.

parts_raw.text: Explain why this result may not be reliable?
Explain the concept of 'mass spectrum' and how it is used to identify bacteria.
Besides organism-related issues, name 3 general advantages and 3 general disadvantages for using MALDI-TOF in a microbiology lab. (Table format: Advantages 1/2/3, Disadvantages 1/2/3)

questions.model_answer:
a) Shigella and Escherichia coli are genetically almost identical (a single genomospecies), so their ribosomal protein mass spectra are essentially indistinguishable. MALDI-TOF cannot reliably separate Shigella from E. coli, nor reliably assign Shigella to species (flexneri vs sonnei vs boydii vs dysenteriae); enteroinvasive E. coli compounds the problem. Confirmation requires biochemical testing plus serotyping with group-specific antisera (or molecular typing). The same limitation applies to other closely related pairs (S. pneumoniae vs viridans streptococci, Burkholderia and Achromobacter species).
b) The colony is mixed with an energy-absorbing matrix on a target plate; a laser pulse desorbs and ionizes the abundant, highly conserved ribosomal and other cytoplasmic proteins. The charged proteins are accelerated through an electric field down a vacuum flight tube, and their time of flight to the detector varies with mass-to-charge ratio (smaller ions arrive first). The plot of ion abundance against m/z, typically 2-20 kDa, is the mass spectrum - a species-level protein fingerprint. Software compares this spectrum with a reference database of validated spectra and returns the best matches with a confidence/log score for genus- and species-level identification.
c) Advantages: (1) Very rapid - identification in minutes rather than 18-48 h of biochemical testing, shortening time to targeted therapy. (2) Very low per-isolate consumable cost and less technologist hands-on time. (3) Broad accurate coverage from a single workflow - Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, anaerobes, fastidious and slow-growing organisms, yeasts and moulds, including organisms that are difficult to identify biochemically; can be applied directly to positive blood culture broth.
Disadvantages: (1) High capital cost of the instrument, plus service contracts, dedicated bench space and staff training. (2) Performance depends entirely on the reference database - organisms absent from or under-represented in the library are misidentified or unidentified, and databases require licensing and updating. (3) It gives identification only, not susceptibility, so conventional AST is still required; it usually needs a pure isolated colony (poor with mixed cultures/direct specimens) and requires ongoing QC and calibration.

parts.text: Name the test.
Describe the mechanism of resistance.
What is the clinical significance?

parts_raw.text: Name the test
Describe mechanism of resistance.
What is the clinical significance?

questions.model_answer:
a) The D-test (double-disk diffusion test for inducible clindamycin resistance), with an erythromycin disk placed 15-26 mm from a clindamycin disk; flattening of the clindamycin zone adjacent to the erythromycin disk gives the D shape.

b) Inducible macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B (MLSb) resistance mediated by an erm gene (ermA, ermC in Staphylococcus aureus; ermB in streptococci). Erm encodes a methylase that methylates adenine in 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit, altering the shared binding site for macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B. Erythromycin is a strong inducer of the methylase while clindamycin is a poor inducer, so the isolate tests clindamycin-susceptible in isolation but demonstrates resistance when erythromycin diffuses across.

c) A positive D-test means the isolate must be reported and treated as clindamycin resistant - erm-expressing mutants can be selected on therapy, causing clinical failure. Clindamycin should therefore not be used for that isolate (choose an alternative such as TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or vancomycin/linezolid for serious disease). A negative D-test in an erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible isolate indicates efflux (msrA) resistance only, and clindamycin can be used.

cohort_answer.text: "D-test" (Double disk diffusion test). Mechanism: inducible clindamycin resistance; erm gene mediates resistance by methylating 23S ribosome, modifying binding site for both macrolides and clindamycin; clindamycin is a poor inducer of the methylase so resistance may not manifest with a clindamycin disc alone in lab, though it can be induced clinically; adding erythromycin can induce resistance, manifesting as D-shaped growth around clindamycin disk. Clinical significance: Positive D-test should be interpreted as clindamycin resistance.

questions.question: Testing for extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs): describe the laboratory methods used.

parts.text: Describe lab methods for testing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs).

parts_raw.text: Describe lab methods for testing ESBLs.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Screening by disk diffusion or broth microdilution: reduced susceptibility to oxyimino-cephalosporins (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime) and/or aztreonam using CLSI screening breakpoints. (2) Phenotypic confirmation by clavulanate synergy: paired disks or MICs of cefotaxime and ceftazidime alone versus with clavulanic acid; >=5 mm zone increase or >=3 twofold (8-fold) MIC decrease with clavulanate confirms ESBL. (3) Double-disk synergy test: cefotaxime/ceftazidime/cefepime disks placed 20-30 mm from an amoxicillin-clavulanate disk; keyhole/champagne-cork expansion of the zone toward clavulanate. (4) ESBL Etest/gradient strips: dual gradient of an oxyimino-cephalosporin alone on one half and with clavulanate on the other; >=3 twofold MIC reduction or a phantom/deformed ellipse is positive. (5) Automated systems (Vitek 2, MicroScan, BD Phoenix) with built-in ESBL confirmation wells. (6) Molecular detection: PCR/multiplex PCR, DNA microarray, or sequencing for blaCTX-M, blaTEM, blaSHV, blaOXA; MALDI-TOF-based hydrolysis assays are an adjunct. Caveats: AmpC hyperproduction masks clavulanate synergy (use cefepime or add cloxacillin); carbapenemases and porin loss can confound. Since current CLSI cephalosporin breakpoints were lowered, ESBL confirmation is used for infection-control/epidemiology rather than to alter reported susceptibility.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100: lowered cephalosporin breakpoints mean routine ESBL confirmation is no longer required to edit susceptibility reports; report as tested.

cohort_answer.text: Disk diffusion: reduced killing by cefotaxime/ceftriaxone/ceftazidime, increased susceptibility in presence of clavulanate. Broth dilution: as above. E-test: clavulanate added to one side of a dual oxyimino-beta-lactam gradient. Automated systems (Vitek, MicroScan, BD Diagnostics). Molecular methods: sequencing, microarray.

questions.question: DNA microarray technology in infectious diseases.

parts.text: Describe the principles of DNA microarray.
Describe two uses in infectious diseases.

parts_raw.text: Describe principles of DNA microarray
Describe 2 uses in ID

questions.model_answer:
a) Principle: thousands of known single-stranded oligonucleotide or cDNA probes are immobilized in an ordered grid on a solid support (glass, silicon, or bead array), each spot of known sequence and location. Nucleic acid extracted from the sample (DNA, or RNA reverse-transcribed to cDNA) is amplified and labelled with a fluorophore, then hybridized to the array; complementary sequences form stable duplexes. Stringent washing removes mismatched/low-affinity binding. A laser scanner measures fluorescence intensity at each spot; signal position identifies the target sequence and intensity is proportional to target abundance. Two-colour designs co-hybridize test and reference samples labelled with different dyes for relative quantification.
b) (1) Multiplex/syndromic pathogen detection and identification directly from clinical specimens (e.g. respiratory or enteric panels, speciation of mycobacteria or fungi) from one hybridization. (2) Genotypic antimicrobial resistance detection, e.g. line-probe/array detection of rpoB, katG/inhA mutations for rifampin and isoniazid resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, or mecA, vanA/vanB, blaKPC/blaNDM. Other accepted uses: strain typing/outbreak investigation via comparative genomic hybridization, and host or pathogen transcriptional profiling.

cohort_answer.text: DNA microarray: small chip (glass/silica) with collection of DNA segments attached; exposure to complementary nucleotide base pairs forms hydrogen bonds (hybridization); washing removes non-specific (weaker) bonds; fluorescent labels added/measured to quantify DNA presence; used more for detecting mRNA presence. Uses in ID: Syndromic pathogen identification; Drug susceptibility testing by detection of resistance genes (e.g. TB INH and RIF); Outbreak investigations (determining strain relatedness).

questions.question: Explain MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry.
questions.question_raw: Explain MALDI-TOF.

parts.text: Describe four key principles of MALDI-TOF and bacterial identification.
List three advantages and three disadvantages.

parts_raw.text: 4 key principles of MALDI-TOF and bacterial identification
List 3 advantages and disadvantages

questions.model_answer:
a) Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-Of-Flight mass spectrometry: (1) Sample preparation: a colony (or processed positive blood culture/urine pellet) is spotted on a metal target and overlaid with an organic matrix (e.g. alpha-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid) that co-crystallizes with the analyte; formic acid/ethanol extraction may be added for yeasts and mycobacteria. (2) Desorption/ionization: a pulsed UV laser is absorbed by the matrix, vaporizing and transferring protons to the analyte, generating predominantly singly charged intact protein ions with minimal fragmentation. (3) Time-of-flight separation: ions are accelerated through a fixed electrical potential in a vacuum flight tube; time to reach the detector varies with the square root of mass-to-charge ratio, so small ions arrive first, giving m/z resolution. (4) Spectral matching: the resulting spectrum, dominated by abundant conserved ribosomal proteins in the 2-20 kDa range, is a species-characteristic peptide mass fingerprint compared against a reference database, with a confidence/log score reported to genus or species level.
b) Advantages: (1) Very rapid - identification in minutes from a colony, shortening time to organism-directed therapy. (2) Low per-test consumable cost and minimal reagent/labour requirement compared with biochemical, molecular, or immunologic identification. (3) Broad and accurate identification across bacteria (including anaerobes and fastidious organisms), yeasts, and moulds, replacing multiple separate identification schemes.
Disadvantages: (1) High capital cost for the instrument and need for database licensing/maintenance. (2) Performance is limited by the reference database - novel, rare, or under-represented organisms are misidentified or unidentified, and closely related taxa are poorly separated (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae vs. S. mitis, Shigella vs. Escherichia coli, some Burkholderia and Mycobacterium complexes). (3) It does not provide antimicrobial susceptibility results (only limited research applications such as beta-lactam hydrolysis assays), and generally requires growth in culture with pure isolates.

cohort_answer.text: Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization-Time of Flight. Sample mixed with matrix on MALDI target, dried/crystallized; desorption/ionization with laser generates singly protonated ions; ions accelerated at fixed potential, separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); charged analytes detected/measured using time of flight (TOF); characteristic spectrum (peptide mass fingerprint, PMF) generated. Advantages: Fast; Accurate; Less expensive than molecular/immunological methods; trained personnel not required. Disadvantages: High initial equipment cost; limited in identifying new strains (requires spectral database with matching PMFs); doesn't provide antibiotic susceptibility.

questions.question: Regarding next-generation sequencing.
questions.question_raw: Regarding next generation sequencing.

parts.text: What are the benefits over other sequencing? List four.
What are four applications of next-generation sequencing in infectious diseases and public health?

parts_raw.text: What are benefits over other sequencing? List 4.
b. What are 4 applications of next generation sequencing in ID and Public Health.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Massively parallel/high-throughput: millions of sequencing reactions run simultaneously, so whole genomes or whole metagenomes are sequenced in a single run rather than one amplicon at a time as with Sanger sequencing. (2) Far lower cost per base and shorter turnaround for large amounts of sequence data. (3) Culture-independent and hypothesis-free: metagenomic sequencing detects unexpected, fastidious, or novel pathogens directly from clinical specimens without a targeted primer set. (4) Much greater resolution and sensitivity: deep coverage detects minority variants/quasispecies and mixed populations (e.g. low-frequency resistance mutations) and gives single-nucleotide-level discrimination between isolates from small amounts of input nucleic acid.
b) (1) Pathogen identification/diagnosis in individual patients, including metagenomic sequencing of CSF, plasma, or tissue for undiagnosed encephalitis, endocarditis, or febrile illness. (2) Outbreak investigation and infection prevention and control: whole-genome sequencing to establish strain relatedness, confirm or refute transmission chains, and identify hospital or foodborne clusters (e.g. PulseNet listeriosis/Salmonella). (3) Antimicrobial resistance detection and surveillance: prediction of resistance phenotype from resistance genes and mutations (e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis rpoB, katG, and full drug-resistance profiling; carbapenemase genes). (4) Population-level molecular surveillance and vaccine/therapeutic development: tracking SARS-CoV-2 and influenza variants, HIV and HCV drug-resistance and transmission networks, serotype replacement after pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccination, and antigen selection for vaccine strain updates.

cohort_answer.text: a) Faster; decreased cost; 'high-throughput' (large amount of DNA sequence data generated); more sensitive/lower DNA needed (amplified). b) ID organisms on individual level; outbreak investigations; surveillance; IP&C purposes; resistance gene monitoring; vaccine development.

parts_raw.text: Describe the laboratory method/test to detect the presence of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) in this organism

The lab technician is worried that this could be a metallo-beta-lactamase. Based on the information you have, give 1 reason why a metallo-beta-lactamase is NOT this strain's mechanism of resistance to beta-lactams

questions.model_answer:
a) Phenotypic confirmation by demonstrating clavulanate inhibition. Screen with ceftazidime and/or cefotaxime (screen positive if MIC >1 mcg/mL or reduced zone). Confirm by combination disk/MIC testing: test cefotaxime and ceftazidime alone versus each combined with clavulanic acid 4 mcg/mL on the same Mueller-Hinton plate. A >=5 mm increase in zone diameter (or a >=3 twofold-dilution, i.e. >=8-fold, decrease in MIC) with clavulanate confirms ESBL production. The double-disk synergy (keyhole) test - a 3rd-generation cephalosporin disk placed 20-30 mm from amoxicillin-clavulanate, with zone extension toward the clavulanate disk - is an equivalent method; molecular detection of blaCTX-M/SHV/TEM can confirm.
b) The isolate is susceptible to meropenem and resistant to aztreonam - the opposite of the metallo-beta-lactamase phenotype. Class B MBLs hydrolyse carbapenems (meropenem would be resistant) but do not hydrolyse the monobactam aztreonam (which would test susceptible unless a separate ESBL/AmpC is present).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 ESBL confirmatory criteria (>=5 mm zone increase / >=3 twofold dilution decrease with clavulanate).

cohort_answer.text: ESBL detection: Double disk diffusion comparing a 3rd gen cephalosporin and a 3rd gen cephalosporin + beta lactamase inhibitor; ≥5mm difference is a positive screen for ESBL. (Additional notes: K. pneumoniae/E. coli without carbapenemases typically have imipenem/meropenem MICs <0.5 mcg/mL; overt carbapenem resistance in these species raises suspicion for carbapenemase; certain patterns in other Enterobacteriaceae (e.g. S to 3rd gen cephalosporins, R to imipenem) suggest SMC/NMC/IMI enzymes in Serratia/Enterobacter; P. aeruginosa/A. baumannii can be carbapenem-resistant without a carbapenemase, but Aztreonam susceptibility with high carbapenem/cephalosporin/penicillin resistance suggests an MBL.) Reason MBL is NOT the mechanism here: 1. Meropenem is sensitive. 2. Aztreonam is resistant. (Class B metallo-beta-lactamases are typically R to 3rd gen cephalosporin, S to Aztreonam, R to Cefoxitin, R to Clavulin - the opposite pattern.)

questions.model_answer:
a) Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae): Gram-positive cocci in chains; grey-white colonies with a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood agar; catalase negative; rapid test - Lancefield group B latex agglutination positive (CAMP test positive, hippurate hydrolysis positive; bacitracin resistant).

questions.model_answer: a) Culture: (1) Slow - HCMV grows slowly and cultures must be held up to 4 weeks before called negative. (2) Requires tissue-culture facilities/expertise and sensitivity depends heavily on specimen quality and viral load. b) Serology IgM/IgG: (1) IgM can persist for weeks to months, limiting its value for dating acquisition of infection. questions.model_answer: a) Standard two-tier testing = a first-tier sonicate EIA/ELISA, and equivocal or positive samples are then confirmed by IgM and IgG Western blot. Modified two-tier testing replaces the Western blot with a second EIA: a sonicate ELISA followed by an IgG VlsE C6-peptide enzyme immunoassay, so no immunoblot (and no IgM testing) is required. b) Advantages: (1) eliminates the subjective, labour-intensive Western blot and the need for IgM testing — the result is a straightforward seropositive/seronegative report; (2) better specificity than the C6 ELISA alone with comparable sensitivity, and it is especially useful to support the diagnosis of early Lyme disease. Disadvantages: (1) it loses the information a Western blot can give about duration of infection or reinfection, so the blot-based approach remains preferable for complex cases; (2) like the sonicate tests, the anti-VlsE response persists for months to years after successful treatment, so seropositivity cannot distinguish active from past infection.

questions.question: Clostridioides difficile testing.

parts.text: Describe the components of C. difficile testing.
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

parts_raw.text: Describe the components of C. diff testing
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

questions.model_answer: a) Tests fall into those detecting the organism/toxin genes versus those detecting free toxin: (1) glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) EIA-detects organism (toxigenic and nontoxigenic), high sensitivity/NPV, a screening step; (2) toxin A/B EIA-detects free toxin, specific but relatively insensitive; (3) NAAT (PCR or LAMP)-detects toxin gene, most sensitive rapid single test; plus reference standards cell cytotoxicity assay and toxigenic culture. These are combined in multistep algorithms: two-step (GDH + toxin EIA) and three-step (GDH + toxin EIA with NAAT arbitration of discrepant results). b) NAAT detects the presence of the toxin gene, not toxin in stool, so used alone it cannot distinguish true CDI from asymptomatic colonization with diarrhea from another cause; it therefore overdiagnoses CDI (apparent rates rise ~50%), and NAAT-alone-positive/toxin-negative patients have lower rates of complications and death.

parts.text: Explain the C. difficile multi-test algorithm and the limitations of NAAT-only testing.

questions.model_answer: Multistep algorithm: begin with a sensitive screen-GDH EIA (or GDH/toxin combination), using its high negative predictive value to report 80-95% of specimens as negative rapidly. In the two-step algorithm GDH is paired with a toxin A/B EIA; when these are discrepant (13-19% of tests) a third step uses NAAT to arbitrate (three-step algorithm), giving rapid turnaround at lower cost than testing every specimen by NAAT. NAAT-only limitation: NAAT detects the toxin gene (i.e., presence of toxigenic organism), not free toxin in stool; used alone it cannot separate true CDI from colonized patients with diarrhea from another cause, causing overdiagnosis (~50% rise in apparent CDI) and detecting patients with milder disease/lower complication and mortality rates.

questions.question: Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. A girl presents with bloody diarrhea and the laboratory reports Shigella flexneri.
questions.question_raw: PM 7. Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. Girl presents with bloody diarrhea and reports Shigella flexneri

parts.text: Why should MALDI-TOF not be used for identification of this organism?
Explain the concept of mass spectrometry and how it allows identification.
Give three advantages and three disadvantages of MALDI-TOF.

parts_raw.text: Why should MALDI-TOF NOT be used for identification of this organism? (1)
Explain the concept of "mass spec" and how it allows identification. (2)
3 advantages and 3 disadvantages of MALDI-TOF (3)

questions.model_answer:
a) Shigella is genetically a biochemically inactive Escherichia coli - the two share essentially identical ribosomal protein spectra, so MALDI-TOF cannot reliably distinguish Shigella species from E. coli; identification requires biochemicals and serotyping/molecular testing.
b) A colony is spotted on a target plate with an energy-absorbing matrix; a laser pulse desorbs and ionizes predominantly abundant ribosomal proteins. The charged proteins are accelerated through a vacuum flight tube in an electric field, and time of flight to the detector varies with mass-to-charge ratio (larger ions fly more slowly). The resulting mass spectrum is a species-specific fingerprint matched against a reference database, generating an identification with a confidence score.
c) Advantages: (1) Very rapid - identification in minutes from a colony, shortening time to optimal therapy. (2) Very low consumable cost per test and less technologist hands-on time than biochemical panels. (3) Accurate and objective across a broad range of bacteria, yeasts, mycobacteria and moulds, including fastidious and anaerobic organisms poorly identified by biochemicals. Disadvantages: (1) High capital cost and need for expertise/maintenance. (2) Identification limited to organisms in the reference database, which is incomplete for some moulds, anaerobes and rare species. (3) Cannot discriminate closely related organisms (Shigella vs E. coli, Streptococcus pneumoniae vs mitis/oralis) and provides no susceptibility data.

cohort_answer.text: Shigella too similar to E. coli (metabolically-challenged E. coli, same ribosomal proteins) - MALDI not reliable. Mass spec: colony placed on matrix, laser causes desorption/ionization of rRNA macroprotein; fragments ionized and accelerated in electromagnetic field, hit detector based on mass:charge ratio (bigger proteins = slower flight, time of flight TOF); spectra unique fingerprint compared to standardized database. Advantages: rapid identification, limited need for lab personnel, highly accurate, less subjective than biochemicals. Disadvantages: organism needs to be in database, does not give susceptibility patterns, expensive machine, unable to identify very closely related organisms (e.g. Strep mitis/oralis, E. coli/Shigella).

questions.model_answer: a) Two-tier (two-step) testing: a sensitive initial screen with GDH EIA (detects organism; high NPV), paired with a toxin A/B EIA (detects free toxin; specific). questions.model_answer:
a) Galactomannan is a heteropolysaccharide (mannan backbone with galactofuranose side chains) that is a major constituent of the Aspergillus cell wall and is released into blood/BAL during active hyphal growth; it is detected by a double-sandwich EIA using the EB-A2 monoclonal antibody against galactofuranose, reported as an optical density index (serum cut-off >=0.5, BAL >=1.0).

b) (1) Fusarium species. (2) Penicillium/Talaromyces marneffei. (3) Histoplasma capsulatum. (4) Paecilomyces (also Trichophyton, Alternaria, and Cryptococcus galactoxylomannan cross-reaction).

c) Highest sensitivity and specificity in profoundly neutropenic haematology patients - acute leukaemia on induction chemotherapy and allogeneic HSCT recipients - screened serially (twice weekly) while not receiving mould-active prophylaxis; in this high-prevalence, angioinvasive-disease population serum sensitivity is roughly 70-80% with specificity ~90%. Performance falls in non-neutropenic hosts (solid-organ transplant, ICU, COPD, chronic granulomatous disease) where BAL galactomannan performs better than serum, and in patients on mould-active azoles/echinocandins.

cohort_answer.text: Description: Galactomannan is a polysaccharide that is a major constituent of Aspergillus cell walls that is released during fungal growth. The isolate is susceptible to clindamycin on phenotypic testing. What additional test should be performed in the local microbiology laboratory?

parts_raw.text: List TWO mechanisms of resistance to this antibiotic.
The isolate is susceptible to clindamycin on phenotypic testing. What additional test should be performed in the local microbiology laboratory?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ribosomal target-site modification — erm-gene-encoded 23S rRNA methylase producing the MLSB phenotype (macrolide–lincosamide–streptogramin B cross-resistance, constitutive or inducible). (2) Active drug efflux — mef-gene-encoded macrolide efflux pump (M phenotype), conferring macrolide resistance while sparing clindamycin.
b) A D-test (erythromycin–clindamycin double-disk induction test) to detect inducible clindamycin resistance, since erm-mediated inducible MLSB isolates can appear clindamycin-susceptible but fail on therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Macrolide resistance mechanisms and the D-test are standard CLSI microbiology, not detailed in this Mandell chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ceftriaxone. (2) Meropenem. (3) Ciprofloxacin. (Ampicillin, ceftazidime, aztreonam, tobramycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are also validated for direct-from-positive-blood-culture disk diffusion with 16-20 h reading.)

b) Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

c) (1) Hand hygiene immediately before insertion. (2) Full maximal sterile barrier precautions - cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves and a full-body sterile drape. (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol, allowed to dry. (4) Optimal site selection - subclavian preferred over internal jugular and avoid the femoral vein in adults; use ultrasound guidance to reduce attempts. (5) Insertion only by trained/competent personnel using a checklist with an empowered observer able to stop the procedure for breaches, and daily review with prompt removal of unnecessary catheters.

questions.question: Candida albicans identification.
questions.question_raw: Candida albicans.

parts.text: What is the rapid test for it?
How do you interpret the test?

parts_raw.text: What is the rapid test for it
How to interpret test?

questions.model_answer:
a) The germ tube test.
b) The yeast is suspended in serum and incubated ~2-3 hours at 35-37 degrees C; a positive test is the appearance of short, non-septate, non-constricted filamentous outgrowths (germ tubes) arising directly from the yeast cell without a constriction at the point of origin. A positive germ tube test gives a rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans (C. dubliniensis also gives a positive result); a negative result points to a non-albicans species, and definitive speciation then relies on other physiologic/molecular methods (e.g., MALDI-TOF MS).

cohort_answer.text: Germ tube test. A rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans can be made by placing organism in serum and observing germ tube formation (small projections appearing within 90 min); used to differentiate C. albicans (and C. dubliniensis) from other Candida spp. Interpretation: sample placed in tube with sheep serum, incubated 2-4h, drop placed on slide with KOH prep - see filamentous outgrowth extending from yeast cells; positive germ tube test = C. albicans (or C. dubliniensis), based on non-constricted germ tube arising from yeast; false-negative and false-positive germ tube formations may occur; remainder of speciation relies on physiologic parameters rather than morphology.

questions.question: An immunocompromised patient has suspected invasive aspergillosis and you order a galactomannan assay.
questions.question_raw: Immunocompromised patient with suspected invasive aspergillosis. You order a galactomannan assay

parts.text: What are three potential factors that could modify the result of the galactomannan assay, and how do they change sensitivity and specificity?
What two investigations would you now consider to confirm a diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 3 potential factors which could modify the result of the galactomannan assay, and how do they change sensitivity and specificity?
What two investigations would you now consider to confirm diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Prior or concurrent anti-mould antifungal therapy – lowers circulating antigen, decreasing sensitivity (false negatives). (2) Sample source – BAL fluid has higher sensitivity than serum. (3) Piperacillin-tazobactam/other antibiotics or, in neonates, cross-reacting Bifidobacterium antigens – cause false positives, decreasing specificity (also colonized COPD/lung-transplant patients).
b) (1) Tissue biopsy showing hyphal invasion with a positive Aspergillus culture (proven disease). (2) Bronchoscopy with BAL for culture/cytology plus chest CT (BAL PCR is more specific than galactomannan).

cohort_answer.text: Decrease sensitivity: patient with CGD/Job syndrome; concomitant use of antimould agents; source of sample from serum. Decrease specificity: PipTazo and AmoxClav (historically, less of an issue now); other fungi (Penicillium, fusarium, histo); chemo (increases false positive due to gut translocation from mucositis); COPD (colonization with aspergillus); neonates (dietary intake or cross-reacting antigens with bacteria like Bifidobacterium); IVIG (1 study found false+ galactomannans post IVIG). Confirmatory investigations: CT chest +/- other imaging depending on symptoms; BAL specimens with tissue specimen for histopathology/cytology and fungal culture; galactomannan.

questions.question: A Brucella plate was manipulated on an open bench in the laboratory.
questions.question_raw: Brucella plate manipulated on open bench.

parts.text: Name three high-risk laboratory activities.
Name three aspects of management of a high-risk exposure.

parts_raw.text: Name three high-risk activities in lab.
Name 3 aspects of management of high risk exposure

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Manipulating an open Brucella culture plate on an open bench outside a biosafety cabinet, or being within about 5 feet of such manipulation. (2) Procedures that aerosolize the organism performed outside a biosafety cabinet - vortexing, centrifuging without sealed carriers, catalase testing, subculturing/streaking, or sniffing plates. (3) Direct personal inoculation or mucosal exposure - needlestick or sharps injury, direct skin contact with a culture (especially non-intact skin), mouth pipetting, or spray/splash into eyes, nose, or mouth.
b) (1) Risk assessment: identify and stratify all laboratory workers present as high- versus low-risk exposures, notify the laboratory director, occupational health, and public health, and confirm the isolate identity/biosafety-level-3 handling going forward. (2) Post-exposure prophylaxis for all high-risk exposures: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID plus rifampin 600 mg PO daily for 3 weeks, started promptly; substitute TMP-SMX DS BID for rifampin if the strain is rifampin-resistant (e.g. RB51) or rifampin is contraindicated; TMP-SMX-based regimens are used in pregnancy and young children. (3) Symptom surveillance and serologic follow-up: instruct workers to report fever or compatible illness and check temperatures for 6 months; obtain baseline serum and repeat Brucella serology at 6, 12, 18, and 24 weeks post-exposure, with blood cultures and treatment for symptomatic seroconversion. Low-risk exposures receive surveillance and serology, with PEP considered if immunocompromised or pregnant.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC MMWR 2008;57(2):39 laboratory Brucella exposure guidance (risk tiers, PEP regimen, 24-week serologic schedule).

cohort_answer.text: High-risk exposure defined as: 1) direct personal exposure (sniffing cultures, direct skin contact, mouth pipetting, inoculation, spraying into eyes/nose/mouth); 2) working on open bench with open Brucella culture plate or close proximity (across open bench or within 5 feet); 3) presence during procedures that might aerosolize organisms (vortexing, catalase testing). Low-risk = present in lab during exposure but not meeting high-risk definition. Management: Step 0: risk assessment for all exposed workers; Step 1: offer PEP to all high-risk exposures (Doxycycline 100mg BID + rifampin 600mg daily x3 weeks, unless rifampin-resistant strain then add TMP-SMX DS BID to doxy; can give PEP to low-risk exposure if immunocompromised/pregnant, sometimes up to 6 months post-exposure); Step 2: surveillance for symptoms x6 months; Step 3: serologic follow-up (baseline, 6, 12, 18, 24 weeks post-exposure). (MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 2008;57(2):39)

questions.question: Clostridioides difficile.
questions.question_raw: C difficile

parts.text: Describe two-tier testing and its rationale.
Why may NAAT not be a good stand-alone test?

parts_raw.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?

questions.model_answer: a) Two-step algorithm: initial EIA for glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH, a common antigen present on all C. difficile, toxigenic and nontoxigenic — high sensitivity, high negative predictive value, lower specificity) paired with an EIA for toxins A/B (high specificity, low sensitivity). Concordant results (both positive or both negative) are reported directly; discrepant results (13%-19%) are arbitrated by NAAT (three-step algorithm). Rationale: GDH rapidly and sensitively rules out C. difficile in 80%-95% of specimens, the toxin EIA confirms toxin production, and NAAT resolves discrepancies — retaining sensitivity and specificity while limiting the cost of testing every specimen by NAAT. b) NAAT detects the toxin gene, not toxin in stool, so it identifies toxigenic organism presence like a toxigenic culture but cannot distinguish active CDI from asymptomatic colonization. Because it is so sensitive, used alone it overdiagnoses (apparent CDI rates rise ~50%); NAAT+/toxin- patients have significantly lower mortality, ICU admission, and colectomy rates than NAAT+/toxin+ patients, so NAAT-alone may capture colonized patients whose diarrhea has another cause.

cohort_answer.text: Step 1 - testing for both glutamate dehydrogenase antigen (found on all C difficile isolates) and toxin A/B using enzyme linked immunoassay: GDH - high sensitivity, lower specificity; Toxins - high specificity, low sensitivity. Step 2 - NAAT testing to confirm presence of C diff toxin gene specific to toxigenic strains (highly sensitive so can rule out infection if negative but does not discriminate between toxin producing and non-toxin producing, colonizing C difficile). Want NAAT testing to follow up if discordant results between GDH and toxin antigens - more expensive but more specific for toxigenic strains, and sensitive

questions.question: A specimen is obtained from a herpes simplex virus lesion.
questions.question_raw: Q87 2023 Day 1. HSV lesion, provide 2 diagnostic tests in micro lab from this specimen aside from PCR. (MICRO)

parts.text: Give two diagnostic tests available in the microbiology laboratory from this specimen other than PCR.

parts_raw.text: 2 diagnostic tests in micro lab from this specimen aside from PCR

questions.model_answer: (1) Viral culture - HSV gives a discernible cytopathic effect in cell culture within 48-96 hours; spin-amplified culture with HSV antigen staining shortens identification to under 24 hours and yields an isolate for typing and phenotypic acyclovir susceptibility testing. (2) Direct antigen detection by immunofluorescent staining of cells scraped from the lesion base (cytologic examination of the scraping for multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions is an insensitive alternative).
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists serology and resistance testing; serology is a blood test, not a test on the lesion swab, and phenotypic resistance testing requires a culture isolate first - culture and antigen detection are the two lesion-specimen answers Mandell supports.

cohort_answer.text: HSV resistance testing; Serology; Culture (suspended due to MPox); STBBI testing.
